Icon on glass – ”The Ascent of the Holy Prophet Elijah into Heaven, with scenes from his life” – (model: Transylvanian workshop, early 19th century).
On 20 July (in midsummer) there is a religious feast awaited with a certain trepidation, because it is most often accompanied by lightning, thunder and torrential rain: Saint Elijah the Tishbite, the Prophet.
Elijah is above all a symbolic figure of identity: the only man to whom the divine power was given to “shut and open the heavens”, the only prophet who appears in the Gospel of Jesus, on Mount Tabor, beside Moses and Jesus in all the glory of the Godhead, knowing God face to face, the man of prayer par excellence. He is recognised as a continuer of monotheism in general and as the forerunner of the second coming of Christ. Elijah is the best known of the prophets of the Bible. He is the only prophet venerated by the three great religions of the world: Judaism, Islam and Christianity. The prophet Elijah holds an important place in Jewish and Islamic mysticism, and also in Orthodox hesychasm: he is the invisible spiritual master who speaks to those called to a direct relationship with the divine world. Elijah is the biblical hero who still influences the whole of culture today, being, par excellence, the whole world's meteorologist on duty."
About the icon:
I painted this icon – after a 19th-century Transylvanian model – in the traditional technique. The icon shows the classic scene of Saint Elijah appearing in the chariot of fire. In the upper part, this chariot appears in the sky, drawn by two red winged horses. The saint stands in the chariot, holding the reins in one hand and in the other the whip with which he drives the horses. The chariot is surrounded by flames. In the lower part, on the ground, Saint Elijah is shown fed by the ravens, and Elisha, with his hands joined in prayer, awaiting Saint Elijah's mantle.

efa00482abeb:
Jesus with the Vine – icon painted on glass (model: Șcheii Brașovului, 19th century)
– The icon is not available; I will paint it again only to order. –

In Romanian iconography there is a theme unique in the originality of its allegorical vision. It is Jesus with the vine (which grows out of His very body), as it appears only in the Romanian icons of Transylvania. It is called “the Icon of the Eucharist” and is considered the most beloved icon of Christ (in Transylvania). The source of this special depiction is Christ's words: "I am the true vine..." (John 15:1). The icon belongs to the altar area, where the bread and wine are prepared for the Holy Liturgy, that is, for Communion. Christ is shown seated on a (dowry) chest [a chest brilliantly linked by the Transylvanian icon painters with the "dowry" of the ancestral faith] before the cross. From His side grows a vine stem full of bunches of grapes, which surrounds Him like a halo, and with His hands Christ presses the grapes into a cup, suggesting the changing of the wine into the blood of the Lord during the Holy Liturgy, and Christ as the source of the life-giving "wine".
4cb16aa8bec5:
~ ” Jesus Christ, King and Great High Priest, flanked by archangels ”~ Icon on glass [model: workshop in Țara Bârsei (1802)]. The icon is painted on glass (21 x 29 cm). Stained fir frame.

> The three Magi from the East (representing all mankind) came to the incarnate Lord (when He was a Child) with gifts (gold, frankincense and myrrh), whose very symbolism explains why Jesus is King and Great High Priest.
 According to Fr. Ionel Popescu (Timișoara), gold was (and still is) offered to kings and emperors as a sign of esteem and respect for their high dignity. Gold is also the symbol of divinity and glory (Matthew: "the shining perfection of His divine Person"). Frankincense is brought as to a great priest, a great high priest. Jesus Christ the Lord also holds the dignity of high priest. Frankincense is an aroma or perfume and suggests the fragrance of His perfect life, wholly without sin. Frankincense (as has been known since antiquity) was used in religious services, in the temple in Jerusalem and in the synagogues. It shows that the Lord Jesus came into the world to serve and not to be served. Myrrh is a bitter plant, which foreshadows the sufferings Christ was to endure, bearing the sins of the world. Myrrh was used in burial rites: the dead were embalmed with myrrh and other spices before being laid in the tomb. The myrrh brought by the Magi symbolises the death and sacrifice of the Lord Jesus for all mankind.

48ef0fbcbe15:
Jesus – the True Vine is a theme found in the Transylvanian peasant icons, evoking the mystery of Holy Communion. The icon illustrates the parable of the vine: “I am the vine, you are the branches”. Jesus presented Himself as the true vine, His Father as the vinedresser who planted it, and His disciples as the branches of this vine. It is an archetype according to which the essential elements of life – food, healing and worship – grew out of the primordial sacrifice.

Hand-painted on glass in tempera and gold leaf, over a pen-and-ink drawing made after the original model. The stained fir frame is also handmade.
0c11373d3eb1:
The theme of this icon (Nicula, 1867) is Saint Nicholas, celebrated on 6 December by both the Orthodox and the Roman Catholic Church. Saint Nicholas is considered the protector of children, especially poor children, and also of sailors, bakers, unmarried girls and the unjustly accused. The tradition of giving gifts began with him.

He was born in the second half of the 3rd century into a wealthy family, in Patara, in the province of Lycia, in the Asian part of today's Turkey. From his youth he felt a calling to the spiritual life. Left without parents, he used the fortune he inherited to help the poor and to build a church. The relics of Saint Nicholas are kept in Bari, in Italy, in a crypt from which a colourless liquid flows, called “Manna”. According to tradition, the local bishop mixes this liquid with water, blesses it and gives it to the faithful.

Hand-painted on glass in tempera and gold leaf, over a pen-and-ink drawing made after the original model. The stained fir frame is also handmade.
01fd642e8b08:
The usual model of the icon of the Virgin and Child, found in both East and West, is the Virgin holding the Child. It contains more than the Mother of God as a person: it is an image and an affirmation of the incarnation and its reality, an affirmation of the Virgin's true and real motherhood.

If you look carefully at the icon, you will see that the Mother of God, holding the Child, never looks at Him. Nor does she look at you, or into the distance: her eyes are always turned inward, in contemplation. Her tenderness is expressed by the shyness of her hands. She holds the Child without embracing Him, as one would hold something holy brought as an offering, and all the tenderness, all the human love, is expressed by the Child, not by the mother. She remains the Mother of God and behaves towards the Child not as towards an ordinary child, but as towards the incarnate Son of God, who became the son of the Virgin; and He, being true man and true God, shows her all the love and tenderness of man and of God.

Hand-painted on glass in tempera and gold leaf, over a pen-and-ink drawing made after the original model. The stained fir frame is also handmade.
62ddc78b2afd:
In Orthodox iconography, Saints Peter and Paul (the first and the last among the Apostles) stand for the Church, or the communion of Israel (Peter) with all the peoples of the world (Paul). The model of the Church held up by the two saints illustrates the words of Jesus: “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build My Church”.

Hand-painted on glass in tempera and gold leaf, over a pen-and-ink drawing made after the original model. The stained fir frame is also handmade.
b05cf790b027:
According to the Book of Genesis (the first book of the Old Testament and of the Bible), Adam and Eve were the first man and the first woman created by God. The moment when the two break the divine commandment and taste from the Tree of Knowledge is a frequent theme in iconography. This theme also attracted the Transylvanian icon painters, who painted the famous Old Testament scene on glass.

Hand-painted on glass in tempera and gold leaf, over a pen-and-ink drawing made after the original model. The stained fir frame is also handmade.
49d075b9f172:
The theme of this icon is Saint George the Great Martyr. He was a Roman soldier of Greek origin, an officer in the guard of Emperor Diocletian, sentenced to death for refusing to renounce the Christian faith. As a martyr, he later became one of the most venerated saints of Christendom. He is remembered by almost all the traditional Churches, usually on 23 April, and is considered the protector of many countries, regions and cities all over the world.

Hand-painted on glass in tempera and gold leaf, over a pen-and-ink drawing made after the original model. The stained fir frame is also handmade.
60180121f228:
The theme of this icon is Saint Paraskeva the New, or Paraskeva of Iași, a saint honoured throughout the Orthodox Church, especially in Romania, Serbia, Greece and Bulgaria. In Romania she is considered the protector of Moldavia and is the most popular of all the saints whose relics lie in the country. Hundreds of parish churches are dedicated to her. Among the people she is also known as Saint Friday. Her feast is on 14 October, when tens of thousands of people come to Iași every year to venerate her holy relics.

Hand-painted on glass in tempera and gold leaf, over a pen-and-ink drawing made after the original model. The stained fir frame is also handmade.

The icon of the Mother of God (Șcheii Brașovului, 1780) depicts the first human being to fulfil the purpose of the Incarnation: the deification of man. It is one of the crowned images of the Queen of the angels, with the Holy Child at her breast and the angels placing the crown on her head.

Hand-painted on glass in tempera and gold leaf, over a pen-and-ink drawing made after the original model. The stained fir frame is also handmade.
